glossary.Pus: Thick fluid of dead white cells, bacteria and tissue debris collecting at a site of infection.
glossary.Staph: Short for Staphylococcus, a group of bacteria that grow in clusters, e.g. Staphylococcus aureus.
glossary.Strep: Short for Streptococcus, a group of bacteria that grow in chains.
glossary.Dental infection: Infection of a tooth or gum, such as a dental abscess, which can spread to nearby structures.
glossary.Immunosuppression: Weakened immune defences, from disease or drugs such as steroids, making infections more likely.
glossary.Steroids: Corticosteroid drugs, such as prednisolone, that dampen inflammation and the immune response.
glossary.Neurosurgery: Surgery on the brain, spine or nerves.
glossary.Space-occupying lesion: Anything taking up room inside the skull, such as a tumour, abscess or bleed, that compresses the brain.
glossary.Altered mental status: A change in alertness, behaviour or thinking, from confusion to drowsiness.
glossary.Seizures: Episodes of abnormal, excessive electrical activity in the brain causing fits or altered awareness.
glossary.Subacute: Developing over days to weeks, slower than acute but faster than chronic.
glossary.Inflammatory markers: Blood tests that rise with inflammation or infection, such as CRP, white cell count and ESR.
glossary.Solitary: A single lesion rather than several.
glossary.Surrounding oedema: Swelling of the brain tissue around a lesion, seen as a dark halo on CT.
glossary.Contrast-enhanced CT: CT scan taken after an iodine dye is injected, so leaky or inflamed tissue lights up.
glossary.MRI: Magnetic resonance imaging; uses magnets and radio waves to give detailed soft-tissue pictures, better than CT for the brain.
glossary.Microbiological diagnosis: Identifying the exact organism by culture or testing of a sample from the infection.
glossary.Drainage: Removing a collection of fluid or pus, surgically or through a needle or tube.
glossary.Blood cultures: Blood samples incubated in bottles to grow and identify bacteria in the bloodstream.
glossary.Broad-spectrum: Antibiotics that kill a wide range of bacteria, used before the organism is known.
glossary.IV: Intravenous; given directly into a vein.
glossary.Cephalosporin: A family of beta-lactam antibiotics; 3rd-generation ones like ceftriaxone cross into the brain well.
glossary.Neurosurgical review: Assessment by the brain surgery team to decide on drainage or other operations.
glossary.Escalation: Calling for more senior help or moving to a higher level of care when a patient worsens.
glossary.Pulmonary filtration: The lung capillaries acting as a sieve that trap clots and bacteria from venous blood.
glossary.Pulmonary capillary filter: The fine lung capillary network that normally traps emboli before blood reaches the systemic arteries.
glossary.Fibrous capsule: A wall of scar-like connective tissue that forms around a mature abscess.
glossary.Contrast imaging: Scans taken after injecting dye so areas with leaky vessels show up brightly.
glossary.Targeted antibiotics: Antibiotics chosen to match the specific organism once it is identified.
glossary.Neurological deficit: Loss of a normal brain or nerve function, such as weakness, numbness or speech problems.
glossary.Focal neuro signs: Deficits pointing to one specific area of the brain, such as one-sided weakness or speech loss.
